steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Mental health: a state of wellbeing where a person can cope with normal stresses, work productively, and contribute to their community (WHO definition). Mental health exists on a continuum - it is not simply 'healthy' or 'ill'.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Mental illness: a condition that affects thinking, feeling or behaviour, causing significant distress. The medical model views mental illness as a disease with biological causes (chemical imbalances, genetics, brain damage) treatable with medication.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The biopsychosocial model (Engel): mental illness results from biological factors (genes, neurotransmitters), psychological factors (cognitions, trauma, learned behaviour), and social factors (poverty, discrimination, social isolation). This is more comprehensive than the medical model alone.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cultural issues in diagnosis: different cultures express and interpret symptoms differently. Culture-bound syndromes (e.g. ataque de nervios in Latin American cultures) are not recognised in Western diagnostic systems. Ethnocentric bias means Western diagnostic criteria may not apply globally.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Compare the medical model with the biopsychosocial model of mental illness. | Explain how cultural factors can affect the diagnosis of mental health problems. | Evaluate whether the medical model is the best approach to understanding mental illness.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Medical model = BIOLOGICAL causes only (drugs treat it). Biopsychosocial = BIO + PSYCHO + SOCIAL (combined treatment). Culture affects diagnosis: different cultures express symptoms differently. Western diagnostic systems may not generalise. Mental health is a CONTINUUM, not a simple healthy/ill divide.
